597099.old: Strong acids (HCl, H2SO4) ionize completely. Weak acids reach an equilibrium that lies mostly on the left, and the acid ionization constant Ka measures how far to the right it goes. Chemists usually quote pKa = −log Ka, which turns a wide range of Ka values into a small, readable number. The rule to remember: the lower the pKa, the stronger the acid. Each unit of pKa is a factor of ten in Ka, so an acid with pKa 10 is about a million times stronger than one with pKa 16.
597099.new: Strong acids (HCl, H2SO4) ionize completely. Weak acids ionize only slightly: the equilibrium lies mostly on the left, and most molecules keep their H. In this course you compare weak acids by ranking them, not with numbers: a stronger acid gives up its H+ more readily, and you can see the difference at the bench by which bases (sodium bicarbonate or sodium hydroxide) it reacts with.

597118.old:
Alcohols are amphoteric substances like water, i.e., they can donate a proton as acid and accept a proton as bases. Like alcohols, the oxygen of carbonyl (\(\ce{C=O}\) group also has two lone pairs and can accept a proton. A strong acid like \(\ce{HCl}\) or \(\ce{H2SO4}\)can protonate an alcohol or a carbonyl group, as shown below.

\[\ce{\underset{pK_a\;-7}{HCl} + R-OH <=>> Cl^{-} + \underset{pK_a\;~-3}{R-OH2^{+}}}\nonumber \]

\[\ce{\underset{pK_a\;-9}{H2SO4} + R-\!\!{\overset{\overset{\Huge\enspace\!{\ce{O}}}|\!\!|\enspace}{\ce{C}}}\!\!-R <=>> HSO4^{-} + \underset{pK_a\;~-7}{R-\!\!\!\!\!\!{\overset{\overset{\Huge\enspace{\overset{\Large{+}}{\ce{O}}\ce{H}}}|\!\!\!\!\!\!|\enspace\enspace}{\ce{C}}}\!\!\!\!\!-R}}\nonumber \]

The acid-base reactions that produce cations by accepting protons, like \(\ce{R-\overset{+}{\ce{O}}\ce{H2}}\) or \(\ce{R-\!\!\!\!\!\!{\overset{\overset{\Huge\enspace{\overset{\Large{+}}{\ce{O}}\ce{H}}}|\!\!\!\!\!\!|\enspace\enspace}{\ce{C}}}\!\!\!\!\!-R}\) and anions by donating protons, like \(\ce{R-O^{-}}\), \(\ce{R-C≡C^{-}}\), \(\ce{R-S^{-}}\), etc. are important intermediates in organic reactions described in the later sections.

Whether a group is ionized depends on the pH around it compared with its pKa. If the pH is at least two units above the pKa of an acid, almost all of it has lost its proton (A−). If the pH is at least two units below the pKa of a protonated amine (R–NH3+), almost all of it keeps its proton.

The following conclusions are drawn by applying the above rules to the functional groups commonly found in cells.

597118.old: You do not need the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation to answer "ionized or not." Subtract: pH minus pKa. Positive by two or more means the acid has lost its proton (carboxylate, RCOO−); negative by two or more means it has kept it (RCOOH); close to zero means a roughly even mixture. The same arithmetic works for the amines of Chapter 7 and the amino acids of Chapter 10.
597118.new: Two rules answer "ionized or not" for almost every molecule in this course. At body pH (about 7.4), write a carboxylic acid as the carboxylate (RCOO−) and an amine as the ammonium ion (RNH3+). In strong acid, such as stomach acid, a carboxylic acid keeps its H (RCOOH). 597165.new: A student explains: “At pH 7.4, the peptide Ala-Lys-Gly has a net charge of 0, because only the two ends of a peptide carry charges and they cancel.” Find the error and correct it.

597165.old: The pI is the pH at which a whole free amino acid has a net charge of zero; it does not tell you the form of one group in a peptide. For the side chain, compare the pH with the side-chain pKa of lysine’s –NH3+, about 10.5. pH 10 is still below 10.5, so most lysine side chains are still protonated (+1). They lose the proton only at higher pH. Review: Section 10.2.
597165.new: Side chains can carry charges too. Lysine is a basic amino acid: its side chain ends in an amine, and like every amine it picks up H+ at body pH, so it is –NH3+ (+1). The N-terminus (+1) and C-terminus (−1) cancel, so the peptide’s net charge is +1, not 0. Review: Section 10.2.
